items.question: Is an alteration of course to port ever permitted under Rule 19(d) for a vessel forward of the beam?
items.good: Yes, if that vessel is being overtaken - the prohibition on altering to port for a vessel forward of the beam explicitly excludes the overtaking case.
items.bad: Yes, if that vessel is being OUTtaken - the prohibition on altering to port for a vessel forward of the beam explicitly excludes the overtaking case.

items.question: Vessel A is exactly 112.5 degrees abaft Vessel B's beam (the boundary angle). Is this overtaking or crossing?
items.good: At exactly the 22.5-degrees-abaft-the-beam boundary (i.e., 112.5 degrees from dead ahead), if there is any doubt as to which situation exists, Rule 13(c) requires assuming it is overtaking and acting accordingly.
items.bad: At exactly the 22.5-degrees-abaft-the-beam boundary (i.e., 112.5 degrees from dead ahead), if there is any doubt as to which situation exists, Rule 13(c) requires assuming it is OUTtaking and acting accordingly.

items.question: You observe: At night, sidelights and sternlight visible, plus a single all-round white light shown above them at the masthead, all separate (not combined). What is the vessel's status?
items.good: A sailing vessel exhibiting the Rule 25(c) optional lights is unlikely here since 25(c) requires red-over-green, not a single white; more likely this is a small power-driven vessel improperly combining lights, or a vessel not under command showing sidelights/sternlight while making way plus an unrelated light - identification is ambiguous and should prompt caution and closer observation/radio contact.
items.bad: A sailing vessel exhibiting the Rule 25(c) optional lights is unlikely here since 25(c) requires red-OUT-green, not a single white; more likely this is a small power-driven vessel improperly combining lights, or a vessel not under command showing sidelights/sternlight while making way plus an unrelated light - identification is ambiguous and should prompt caution and closer observation/radio contact.

items.question: Define 'sternlight'.
items.good: A white light placed as nearly as practicable at the stern, showing an unbroken light over an arc of 135 degrees, fixed to show 67.5 degrees from right aft on each side.
items.bad: A white light placed as nearly as practicable at the stern, showing an unbroken light OUT an arc of 135 degrees, fixed to show 67.5 degrees from right aft on each side.

items.question: Two vessels detect each other on radar in clear visibility at 10 miles' range, but cannot yet see each other visually due to darkness and distance limitations of the eye (not restricted visibility). Does Section II apply yet?
items.good: Not yet - Section II applies only once the vessels are in sight of one another (i.e., can be observed visually), so until visual sighting occurs, Section I (Rules 4-10) governs; once visually sighted, Rules 11-18 apply.
items.bad: Not yet - Section II applies only once the vessels are in sight of one another (i.e., can be observed visually), so until visual sighting occurs, Section I (Rules 4-10) gOUTns; once visually sighted, Rules 11-18 apply.

items.question: Does Rule 18 apply to two power-driven vessels approaching in a crossing situation?
items.good: Rule 18 does not itself resolve that encounter - between two ordinary power-driven vessels, Rule 15 (crossing) governs directly; Rule 18's category hierarchy matters when the two vessels are of different types (e.g., power-driven vs. sailing, or vs. NUC/RAM/fishing).
items.bad: Rule 18 does not itself resolve that encounter - between two ordinary power-driven vessels, Rule 15 (crossing) governs directly; Rule 18's category hierarchy matters when the two vessels are of different types (e.g., power-driven vs. NUC/RAM/fishing).

items.question: Vessel A (power-driven) sights Vessel B (power-driven) broad on the port bow, bearing -45 degrees relative, with risk of collision, both in sight of one another. Who is give-way and what must each do?
items.good: Vessel B is the give-way vessel (Rule 15, since A is on B's starboard side) and must keep well clear, typically altering to starboard to pass astern of A. Vessel A is the stand-on vessel and must maintain course and speed under Rule 17(a)(i), only deviating under Rule 17(a)(ii)/(b) if B fails to act or collision becomes otherwise unavoidable.
items.bad: Vessel B is the give-way vessel (Rule 15, since A is on B's starboard side) and must keep well clear, typically altering to starboard to pass astern of A. Vessel A is the stand-on vessel and must maintain course and speed under the applicable regulations(a)(i), only deviating under the applicable regulations(a)(ii)/(b) if B fails to act or collision becomes otherwise unavoidable.

items.question: Vessel A (power-driven) sights Vessel B (power-driven) just abaft the starboard beam, bearing 100 degrees relative, with risk of collision, both in sight of one another in clear visibility. Who is give-way and what must each do?
items.good: Vessel A is the give-way vessel (Rule 15, since B is on A's starboard side) and must take early and substantial action to keep well clear (Rule 16), normally by altering course to starboard to pass astern of B, avoiding crossing ahead if circumstances admit. Vessel B is the stand-on vessel and must keep her course and speed (Rule 17(a)(i)) unless it becomes apparent A is not taking appropriate action, or in extremis under Rule 17(b).
items.bad: Vessel A is the give-way vessel (Rule 15, since B is on A's starboard side) and must take early and substantial action to keep well clear (Rule 16), normally by altering course to starboard to pass astern of B, avoiding crossing ahead if circumstances admit. Vessel B is the stand-on vessel and must keep her course and speed (the applicable regulations(a)(i)) unless it becomes apparent A is not taking appropriate action, or in extremis under the applicable regulations(b).

items.question: Vessel A, in fog, detects Vessel B by radar 30 degrees forward of her port beam on a steady bearing with decreasing range; A and B are not overtaking. What alterations should A avoid, per Rule 19(d)?
items.good: A should avoid altering course to port (since B is forward of her beam and this is not an overtaking case) and should avoid altering towards B if B were instead abeam or abaft the beam (not applicable here since B is forward). A safe option would typically be an alteration to starboard and/or reduction of speed.
items.bad: A safe option would typically be an alteration to starboard and/or reduction of speed.

items.question: Vessel B is the stand-on vessel in a crossing situation but Vessel A (give-way) has taken no avoiding action and the range is closing rapidly. What may/must Vessel B do?
items.good: Under Rule 17(a)(ii), B may take action to avoid collision by her own manoeuvre as soon as it becomes apparent A is not taking appropriate action. If collision cannot be avoided by A's action alone, Rule 17(b) requires B to take such action as will best aid to avoid collision.
items.bad: If collision cannot be avoided by A's action alone, Rule 17(b) requires B to take such action as will best aid to avoid collision.

items.question: Vessel A (give-way, power-driven) is crossing with Vessel B (stand-on) on A's starboard bow. A third vessel, C, is also in sight, ahead of A on a steady bearing. How should A's Rule 16 action account for C?
items.good: A's action to comply with Rule 16 (avoid B) must also comply with Rule 8(d)/(f) - it must not create a close-quarters situation or risk of collision with C. A should choose an alteration (typically to starboard, astern of B) that keeps her clear of both B and C simultaneously; if no single safe manoeuvre exists, A should reduce speed or stop under Rule 8(e) while reassessing.
items.bad: A should choose an alteration (typically to starboard, astern of B) that keeps her clear of both B and C simultaneously; if no single safe manoeuvre exists, A should reduce speed or stop under Rule 8(e) while reassessing.
